# System ops [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/sysops.html\#system-ops "Link to this heading")

System ops start with a double-colon `::` and must appear alone in a script.
In the following, we explain what each system op does, and the arguments they expect.

## Explain [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/sysops.html\#explain "Link to this heading")

::explain{<QUERY>}

A single query is enclosed in curly braces. Query options are allowed but ignored.
The query is not executed, but its query plan is returned instead.
Currently, there is no specification for the return format,
but you can decipher the result after reading [Query execution](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/execution.html).

## Ops for stored relations [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/sysops.html\#ops-for-stored-relations "Link to this heading")

::relations

List all stored relations in the database

::columns<REL\_NAME>

List all columns for the stored relation `<REL_NAME>`.

::indices<REL\_NAME>

List all indices for the stored relation `<REL_NAME>`.

::describe<REL\_NAME><DESCRIPTION>?

Describe the stored relation `<REL_NAME>` and store it in the metadata.
If `<DESCRIPTION>` is given, it is stored as the description, otherwise the existing description is removed.
The description can be shown with `::relations`. It serves as the documentation and signpost for humans and AI.

::remove<REL\_NAME>(,<REL\_NAME>)\*

Remove stored relations. Several can be specified, joined by commas.

::rename<OLD\_NAME>-><NEW\_NAME>(,<OLD\_NAME>-><NEW\_NAME>)\*

Rename stored relation `<OLD_NAME>` into `<NEW_NAME>`. Several may be specified, joined by commas.

::index...

Manage indices. See [Stored relations and transactions](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/stored.html) for more details.

::hnsw...

Manage HNSW indices. See [Proximity searches](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/vector.html) for more details.

::show\_triggers<REL\_NAME>

Display triggers associated with the stored relation `<REL_NAME>`.

::set\_triggers<REL\_NAME>...

Set triggers for the stored relation `<REL_NAME>`. This is explained in more detail in [Stored relations and transactions](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/stored.html).

::access\_level<ACCESS\_LEVEL><REL\_NAME>(,<REL\_NAME>)\*

Sets the access level of `<REL_NAME>` to the given level. The levels are:

- `normal` allows everything,

- `protected` disallows `::remove` and `:replace`,

- `read_only` additionally disallows any mutations and setting triggers,

- `hidden` additionally disallows any data access (metadata access via `::relations`, etc., are still allowed).


The access level functionality is to protect data from mistakes of the programmer,
not from attacks by malicious parties.

## Monitor and kill [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/sysops.html\#monitor-and-kill "Link to this heading")

::running

Display running queries and their IDs.

::kill<ID>

Kill a running query specified by `<ID>`. The ID may be obtained by `::running`.

## Maintenance [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/sysops.html\#maintenance "Link to this heading")

::compact

Instructs Cozo to run a compaction job.
Compaction makes the database smaller on disk and faster for read queries.

# Types [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/datatypes.html\#types "Link to this heading")

## Runtime types [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/datatypes.html\#runtime-types "Link to this heading")

Values in Cozo have the following _runtime types_:

- `Null`

- `Bool`

- `Number`

- `String`

- `Bytes`

- `Uuid`

- `List`

- `Vector`

- `Json`

- `Validity`


`Number` can be `Float` (double precision) or `Int` (signed, 64 bits). Cozo will auto-promote `Int` to `Float` when necessary.

`List` can contain any number of mixed-type values, including other lists.

`Vector` have fixed length and contain floats. There are two versions: F32 vectors and F64 vectors.

Cozo sorts values according to the above order, e.g. `null` is smaller than `true`, which is in turn smaller than the list `[]`.

Within each type values are _compared_ according to:

- `false < true`;

- `-1 == -1.0 < 0 == 0.0 < 0.5 == 0.5 < 1 == 1.0`;

- Lists are ordered lexicographically by their elements;

- Bytes are compared lexicographically;

- Strings are compared lexicographically by their UTF-8 byte representations;

- UUIDs are sorted in a way that UUIDv1 with similar timestamps are near each other.
This is to improve data locality and should be considered an implementation detail.
Depending on the order of UUID in your application is not recommended.

- Json values are compared by their string representation, which is a bit arbitrary and you should not rely on the order.

- Validity is introduced for the sole purpose of enabling [time travel](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/timetravel.html) queries.


Warning

`1 == 1.0` evaluates to `true`, but `1` and `1.0` are distinct values,
meaning that a relation can contain both as keys according to set semantics.
This is especially confusing when using JavaScript, which converts all numbers to float,
and python, which does not show a difference between the two when printing.
Using floating point numbers in keys is not recommended if the rows are accessed by these keys
(instead of accessed by iteration).

## Literals [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/datatypes.html\#literals "Link to this heading")

The standard notations `null` for the type `Null`, `false` and `true` for the type `Bool` are used.

Besides the usual decimal notation for signed integers,
you can prefix a number with `0x` or `-0x` for hexadecimal representation,
with `0o` or `-0o` for octal,
or with `0b` or `-0b` for binary.
Floating point numbers include the decimal dot (may be trailing),
and may be in scientific notation.
All numbers may include underscores `_` in their representation for clarity.
For example, `299_792_458` is the speed of light in meters per second.

Strings can be typed in the same way as they do in JSON using double quotes `""`,
with the same escape rules.
You can also use single quotes `''` in which case the roles of double quotes and single quotes are switched.
There is also a “raw string” notation:

```
___"I'm a raw string"___
```

Copy to clipboard

A raw string starts with an arbitrary number of underscores, and then a double quote.
It terminates when followed by a double quote and the same number of underscores.
Everything in between is interpreted exactly as typed, including any newlines.
By varying the number of underscores, you can represent any string without quoting.

There is no literal representation for `Bytes` or `Uuid`.
Use the appropriate functions to create them.
If you are inserting data into a stored relation with a column specified to contain bytes or UUIDs,
auto-coercion will kick in and use `decode_base64` and `to_uuid` for conversion.

Lists are items enclosed between square brackets `[]`, separated by commas.
A trailing comma is allowed after the last item.

There are no literal representations for `Vector` or `Validity`. Use the function `vec` to convert a list to a vector.

Json objects are enclosed between curly brackets `{}`, with key-value pairs separated by commas. For all other Json subtypes, use the function `json` to convert normal values to them.

## Column types [\#](https://docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/datatypes.html\#column-types "Link to this heading")

The following _atomic types_ can be specified for columns in stored relations:

- `Int`

- `Float`

- `Bool`

- `String`

- `Bytes`

- `Uuid`

- `Json`

- `Validity`


There is no `Null` type. Instead, if you put a question mark after a type, it is treated as _nullable_,
meaning that it either takes value in the type or is null.

Two composite types are available. A _homogeneous list_ is specified by square brackets,
with the inner type in between, like this: `[Int]`.
You may optionally specify how many elements are expected, like this: `[Int; 10]`.
A _heterogeneous list_, or a _tuple_, is specified by round brackets, with the element types listed by position,
like this: `(Int, Float, String)`. Tuples always have fixed lengths.

Vectors are also valid as component types and is written in the syntax `<F32; 1024>` for a 1024-element F32 vector. The type can also be F64.

A special type `Any` can be specified, allowing all values except null.
If you want to allow null as well, use `Any?`.
Composite types may contain other composite types or `Any` types as their inner types.

<skill name="session-navigation" filePath="builtin:session-navigation">
# Session navigation

Find your way around past Droid sessions. Maybe you want to pick up where you left off, find that thing you did last week, or just see what's been happening in a project.

## Where sessions live

Sessions are in `~/.factory/sessions/`, organized by project folder. Each project gets its own directory with the path encoded (slashes become dashes):

```
~/.factory/sessions/
├── -Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/
│   ├── <uuid>.jsonl
│   └── <uuid>.settings.json
├── -Users-enoreyes-code-projects-api/
│   ├── <uuid>.jsonl
│   └── <uuid>.settings.json
└── ...
```

Two files per session:

**The conversation** (`.jsonl`): Each line is a JSON object. First line has metadata (session id, title, working directory). Rest is the back-and-forth: user messages, assistant responses, tool calls.

**The settings** (`.settings.json`): Stats about the session. Which model, how long it ran, token counts, autonomy mode.

## Finding sessions

### List project folders

```bash
# See all project folders with sessions
ls ~/.factory/sessions/

# Find folders for a specific project (partial match)
ls ~/.factory/sessions/ | grep "myapp"
```

### Recent sessions in a project

```bash
# List sessions by date for a project
ls -lt ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/

# Get titles of recent sessions
for f in $(ls -t ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/*.jsonl | head -10); do
  echo "=== $f ==="
  head -1 "$f" | jq -r '.title // "Untitled"'
done
```

### Search by content

```bash
# Search across ALL sessions
rg "authentication" ~/.factory/sessions/

# Search within a specific project
rg "bug fix" ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/

# See matches in context
rg -C 2 "login" ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-projects-api/
```

### Find which project has sessions about something

```bash
# Which projects have sessions mentioning "redis"?
rg -l "redis" ~/.factory/sessions/ | cut -d'/' -f1-5 | sort -u
```

## Reading a session

Once you've found a session file:

```bash
# The metadata (title, working directory)
head -1 ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/<uuid>.jsonl | jq .

# Session stats (model, tokens, duration)
cat ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/<uuid>.settings.json | jq .

# How long was this conversation?
wc -l ~/.factory/sessions/-Users-enoreyes-code-work-myapp/<uuid>.jsonl
```

User messages have `"role": "user"`, assistant responses have `"role": "assistant"`. Tool calls show what commands ran and what files got touched.

## Common situations

**"What did I work on in this project?"**
List that project's session folder, check dates, read through the conversation files.

**"Find that session where we fixed the login bug"**
Search for "login" or "auth" across sessions. Once you find it, read the conversation.

**"Resume what I was doing"**
Find the session, read through what happened, summarize the key decisions before continuing.

**"How much have I been using Droid?"**
The settings files have token counts and active time. Sum across sessions if needed.

## Tips

Use `rg` (ripgrep) instead of grep. It's faster and handles nested folders better.

Project paths have slashes replaced with dashes. `/Users/me/code/app` becomes `-Users-me-code-app`.

The session title isn't always helpful. Sometimes you need to read the conversation to know what it was about.

Sessions can contain sensitive stuff. Be careful about what you surface.
</skill>

# Requirements — cozo-store-and-subid-routing

## Scope

Seven coordinated changes that complete the structured-data and semantic projection
pipeline:

**A.** CozoDB incus container running `cozoserver` (RocksDB engine) as the
structured/temporal projection target, registered in the subid registry.

**B.** `CozoPlugin` rewired from its embedded `/var/lib/opdbus/cognitive.db`
to the containerized cozoserver through the Ghostbridge path (same pattern
as the qdrant plugin).

**C.** Socket provisioning: gated `createunixsocket` mutations that register
identity tags + port lists for qdrant, cozo, netmaker-mq, and netmaker-ui
onto the shared `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock`, projected onto the
WG-gated SESSION bus.

**D.** Xray config regeneration: fix the stale `qdrant-out → TCP :6334`
dead-end; all `unix`-backend services (qdrant, cozo, netmaker-*) emit
`to-{tag} → grpc-bridge :50051` outbounds via the `route_to_outbound(Unix)`
path that already exists in `schema_bridge.rs`.

**E.** Gemma subid router: event-driven consumer of `MutationEngine`
`StateChange` / `EventChain` that materializes each mutation into the
correct store(s) — chain (always), cozo (structural/relational), qdrant
(content-bearing only) — based on subid category classification.

**F.** Selective auto-embedding: the qdrant sink of the router applies a
content-bearing gate before calling Voyage — structural subids (`mut`,
`prj`, `sch`, `src`) are **never** embedded; only `obs` and `exp` subids
carrying narrative/semantic content are embedded.

**G.** Battle-test plan: batch-embed the remaining un-embedded corpus
(compliance corpora, code/spec collections) through the live path, skipping
already-present Qdrant point IDs to avoid double-spend.

---

## Functional Requirements

### FR-A1 — Cozo incus container with RocksDB engine

WHEN the deploy script runs,
THE SYSTEM SHALL provision an incus container named `cozo` with:
- no NIC (network-isolated, UDS-only access via container.sock);
- a dedicated storage volume mounted at `/data/cozo/rocksdb` inside the container;
- `cozoserver` built with the `--features storage-rocksdb` flag, data directory
  pointing at `/data/cozo/rocksdb`, HTTP JSON API bound to `127.0.0.1:9070` inside

Update the spec files in `.kiro/specs/cozo-store-and-subid-routing/` (requirements.md, design.md, tasks.md) to reflect the following completed work and remaining work, with full compliance integration.

## Already completed (do NOT re-specify as new work)

1. **qdrant.rs plugin** — Created at `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/qdrant.rs`. Schema derived from Qdrant's official OpenAPI spec (`qdrant/qdrant/docs/redoc/master/openapi.json`). Fields mirror CollectionInfo, CollectionConfig, VectorParams, HnswConfig, OptimizersConfig, CollectionStatus (green/yellow/grey/red), Distance (Cosine/Euclid/Dot/Manhattan), Datatype (float32/uint8/float16/turbo4). OSCAL subids integrated: `sch.software.plugin.qdrant.schema@v1`, `src.software.plugin.qdrant.{http-endpoint,grpc-endpoint}@v1`, `obs.software.plugin.qdrant.{version,title,commit,collections,cluster-status,telemetry}@v1`. Calls `ensure_category_metadata_fields` for src.* accountability fields (source_system, source_ref).

2. **cozo.rs plugin** — Created at `crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/cozo.rs`. Schema derived from CozoDB official docs (`docs.cozodb.org/en/latest/`). Fields mirror `::relations`, `::columns`, `::indices` system ops output with types (Int, Float, Bool, String, Bytes, Uuid, Json, Validity, Any), engines (mem/sled/rocksdb/sqlite), access levels (normal/protected/read_only/hidden). OSCAL subids integrated: `sch.software.plugin.cozo.schema@v1`, `src.software.plugin.cozo.{engine,path}@v1`, `obs.software.plugin.cozo.{version,relations,indices,hnsw-indices,triggers,running-queries}@v1`. Calls `ensure_category_metadata_fields`.

3. **query_current_state removed** — Removed from `StatePlugin` trait in `op-state/src/plugin.rs` and all 66+ plugin implementations. The plugin IS the schema — schema in `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/` is the one source of truth. No stubs, no false confidence. `verify_state` returns `Ok(true)`, `create_checkpoint` uses `json!(null)` for state_snapshot, tests calling `query_current_state` removed.

4. **cognitive-mcp refactored** — `db_path` field removed from `CognitiveMcpConfig` (owned by cozo plugin's `path` field). `qdrant` and `cozo` added as plugin dependencies via `.dependency("qdrant").dependency("cozo")`. Collection field descriptions updated to reference qdrant plugin.

5. **JSON Schema dialect fixed** — Changed fake `https://json-schema.org/v1/2026` (404) to real `https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema` in `op-state-store/src/plugin_schema.rs`.

## Remaining work to spec (update tasks, design, requirements)

### A. CozoDB incus container with RocksDB engine
- Provision incus container named `cozo` with no NIC (network-isolated, UDS-only)
- `cozoserver` built with `--features storage-rocksdb`, data at `/data/cozo/rocksdb`
- HTTP JSON API on `127.0.0.1:9070` inside container
- Access via `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock` only (same pattern as qdrant)
- Subid registry entry: `src.service.cozo-serve@v1`

### B. CozoPlugin rewired to container
- Remove embedded engine from CozoPlugin
- Add HTTP client to cozoserver through Ghostbridge path
- Same pattern as qdrant plugin (endpoint, not db path)

### C. Socket provisioning
- `createunixsocket` mutations register identity tags + port lists for qdrant, cozo, netmaker-mq, netmaker-ui
- All onto shared `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock`
- Projected onto WG-gated SESSION bus

### D. Xray config regeneration
- Fix stale `qdrant-out → TCP :6334` dead-end
- All unix-backend services emit `to-{tag} → grpc-bridge :50051` outbounds
- Via `route_to_outbound(Unix)` path in `schema_bridge.rs`

### E. Gemma subid router
- Event-driven consumer of MutationEngine StateChange/EventChain
- Classify mutation subid into seven OSCAL categories (src, prj, sch, mut, obs, evt, exp)
- Route to correct stores: chain (always), cozo (structural/relational), qdrant (content-bearing only)
- `SubidRouter` struct in `crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/subid_router.rs`

### F. Selective auto-embedding
- Qdrant sink applies content-bearing gate before calling Voyage
- Structural subids (mut, prj, sch, src) are NEVER embedded
- Only obs and exp subids carrying narrative/semantic content are embedded

### G. Battle-test plan
- Batch-embed remaining un-embedded corpus (compliance corpora, code/spec collections)
- Through live path, skipping already-present Qdrant point IDs

## Compliance requirements (MUST be in requirements.md and tasks.md)

### OSCAL subid taxonomy
- Every new D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool carries a subid
- Format: `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`
- Seven categories: src, prj, sch, mut, obs, evt, exp
- mut.* records must carry actor_id and capability_id
- evt.* records must carry event_id or event_hash
- All subids registered in canonical registry, uniqueness enforced in CI

### NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 control mapping
- Cozo container provisioning: AU-2 (audit events), AU-6 (audit review), SC-8 (transmission integrity via WG)
- Socket provisioning: AC-3 (access enforcement), SC-8 (transmission security)
- Xray route regeneration: SC-7 (boundary protection), AC-4 (information flow enforcement)
- Subid router: AU-6, AU-12 (audit generation), SI-7 (software/firmware integrity)
- Auto-embedding: AC-3, SC-8, AU-6 (content-bearing audit trail)
- Control references in subid registry entries: `control_source`, `control_refs`, `statement_refs` fields

### EU AI Act considerations
- Embedding pipeline is a "limited risk" AI system under Article 50 (transparency)
- Content-bearing subid gate (F) provides auditability for embedding decisions
- Battle-test plan (G) must document which corpora were embedded and why
- Gemma subid router classification (E) must be deterministic and auditable

### GDPR considerations
- Cozo relations store no PII (same pattern as existing `users` relation: wg_pubkey-keyed, no email)
- Qdrant embeddings of compliance corpora: document lawful basis (legitimate interest, Art 6(1)(f))
- Socket provisioning does not expose personal data externally (WG-gated, UDS-only)
- Audit events in cozo: `actor` field is wg_pubkey, not personal identifier

### Accountability loop
- X-Ghostbridge-Footprint and X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID injected into Xray gRPC metadata
- Every mutation through the subid router carries the footprint and trace ID
- Audit page UI displays chatbot actions and Qdrant semantic search for user confrontation
- Cozo audit_event relation: `event_id => subid, plugin_id, operation, actor, verdict, reason, control_ref, timestamp`

## Spec file structure

Update these three files:
- `requirements.md` — functional requirements with FR-XX IDs, compliance section with NIST/EU AI Act/GDPR mappings
- `design.md` — crate/file map, system topology, subid router design, compliance architecture
- `tasks.md` — ordered tasks T-XX with files, work, acceptance criteria, compliance checkpoints

- `d67c2824` — qdrant and cozo plugins created

- Qdrant sink applies content-bearing gate before calling Voyage

## Compliance requirements (MUST be in requirements.md and tasks.md)

### Compliance Engine Architecture (The "Law Firm")
Four dedicated compliance personas evaluate every mutation before it reaches cozo/qdrant:

1. **Olivia Scal (OSCAL Managing Partner)** — Validates subid taxonomy compliance. Every mutation must carry a valid subid in the canonical registry. Rejects mutations with unregistered or malformed subids. Maps `control_source` / `control_refs` / `statement_refs` to NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 controls.

2. **E.U.gene Risk (EU AI Act Counsel)** — Classifies AI system risk level. The embedding pipeline (F) is "limited risk" under Article 50 (transparency obligations). Requires documentation of which content was embedded and why. The content-bearing subid gate (structural subids never embedded) satisfies the auditability requirement. Battle-test plan (G) must produce a transparency log.

3. **Penny Privacy (GDPR Engine)** — Validates data minimization. Cozo relations must not store PII (wg_pubkey-keyed identities, not emails). Qdrant embeddings must document lawful basis (Art 6(1)(f) legitimate interest for system security/audit). Socket provisioning must not expose personal data (WG-gated, UDS-only). Privacy router user accounts (`privacy_users` relation) require explicit user directive for PII storage.

4. **Reggie O.P.A. (Cloud Prosecutor)** — Open Policy Agent integration. Evaluates `compliance_rule` relation in cozo before every mutation. Rules are `plugin x op → action(Deny/Allow) + reason + control_ref`. If denied, mutation is rejected, audit_event written with `verdict: "deny"`, and the caller receives the reason.

### Compliance gate flow (per mutation)
1. Mutation arrives at MutationEngine with `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint` and `X-Ghostbridge-Trace-ID` headers
2. SubidRouter classifies subid (or infers from plugin + member fields)
3. Reggie O.P.A. queries `compliance_rule` in cozo: `?[action, reason, control_ref] := *compliance_rule{plugin: $plugin, op: $op, ...}`
4. If `action == "Deny"`: mutation rejected, `audit_event` written with `verdict: "deny"`, caller receives reason + control_ref
5. If `action == "Allow"` (or no rule exists): mutation proceeds
6. Olivia Scal validates subid is registered in `subid_registry`
7. Penny Privacy checks data minimization for the payload
8. E.U.gene Risk classifies if content-bearing (for embedding gate)
9. Mutation written to `mutation_audit` and `audit_event` relations in cozo
10. If content-bearing (obs/exp subid with non-empty text): embedded via Voyage, upserted to qdrant

### OSCAL subid taxonomy
- Every new D-Bus object, plugin, schema, mutation, event, and tool carries a subid
- Format: `<category>.<component-type>.<subject>.<verb>[.<facet>][@vN]`
- Seven categories: src, prj, sch, mut, obs, evt, exp
- Component-types reuse OSCAL vocabulary: software, service, network, hardware, process-procedure, standard, validation, policy, plan, guidance, physical, this-system, system, interconnection
- mut.* records must carry actor_id and capability_id
- evt.* records must carry event_id or event_hash
- All subids registered in canonical registry (`deploy/config/subid-registry.json`), uniqueness enforced in CI
- subid is immutable per subject — if meaning changes, create new subject with @vN

### NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 control mapping (per component)

| Component | Controls | How |
|---|---|---|
| Cozo container (A) | AU-2, AU-6, AU-12, SC-8 | Audit event generation, review, transmission integrity via WG tunnel |
| CozoPlugin rewire (B) | AU-6, SC-8, SI-7 | Audit review via introspection, transmission security, software integrity |
| Socket provisioning (C) | AC-3, SC-7, SC-8 | Access enforcement (WG-gated), boundary protection (UDS-only), transmission security |
| Xray route regen (D) | SC-7, AC-4, AC-3 | Boundary protection, information flow enforcement, access enforcement |
| Subid router (E) | AU-6, AU-12, SI-7, AC-3 | Audit generation, review, software integrity, access enforcement |
| Auto-embedding (F) | AU-6, AC-3, SC-8, AU-12 | Content-bearing audit trail, access enforcement, transmission security |
| Battle-test (G) | AU-6, AU-12, CA-2 | Audit review, generation, control assessment |

Control references stored in subid registry entries:
- `control_source`: e.g., "NIST_SP_800_53_R5"
- `control_refs`: e.g., ["AU-6", "AU-12", "SC-8"]
- `statement_refs`: e.g., ["AU-6(a)", "AU-12.1"]

### EU AI Act considerations
- Embedding pipeline (F) is "limited risk" AI system under Article 50 (transparency obligations)
- Content-bearing subid gate provides auditability: structural subids (mut, prj, sch, src) are NEVER embedded; only obs/exp with narrative content
- Battle-test plan (G) must produce a transparency log: which corpora were embedded, subid classification, timestamp, actor
- Gemma subid router classification (E) must be deterministic and auditable — same subid always routes to same stores
- Article 50(2): users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system — chatbot accountability page satisfies this
- Article 12(1): technical documentation — the spec files themselves (requirements.md, design.md, tasks.md) serve as documentation

### GDPR considerations
- Cozo relations store no PII by default (wg_pubkey-keyed `users` relation, no email)
- `privacy_users` relation stores PII only per explicit user directive (Art 9 special category requires explicit consent)
- Qdrant embeddings of compliance corpora: lawful basis is legitimate interest (Art 6(1)(f)) for system security and audit
